voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.

beats.vo: In July of fifteen eighteen, in the city of Strasbourg, a woman named Frau Troffea stepped into the street and began to dance. No music. No reason anyone could see. She simply would not stop.
Within a week, thirty more had joined her. Within a month, as many as four hundred people were dancing — through the summer heat, day and night, until their feet bled and they collapsed.
The city could not explain it, so they tried to cure it with more dancing: a stage, hired musicians, guild halls cleared out for the afflicted. It only made things worse.
You will read that it killed hundreds — fifteen people a day, at its worst. But that number comes from writers a century later. Strasbourg's own records from 1518 never mention a single death.

The best guess now isn't poison, or plague. It's fear — a city starved and terrified, dancing itself into a trance it could not leave. Four hundred people danced for weeks. What it cost them was never written down.
